1.pericope_label: Abijam’s short reign: the name, the lamp left for David’s sake, and two textual cruxes

schools.summary: Henry reads the difference of the king’s name as a deliberate disgrace, since in Chronicles, where no wickedness is laid to his charge, he is Abijah, my father is the Lord, while here, where his faults are told, the name of God is taken from his name; he alone gives a reason for the brevity of the reign, that the king was made proud by his great victory and cut off to make way for a better son; he takes Abishalom for David’s son Absalom, the more readily because two others of Rehoboam’s wives were his near relations; he turns the lamp against the heir, since it aggravates the sin of a degenerate seed to fare the better for their ancestors’ piety and not imitate it; and on the exception made in David’s praise he calls it a remaining blot and a bar in his escutcheon, covering both the murder and the debauching of the wife, observing that the reproach was not wiped away though the guilt was, yet that the sin repented of did not throw him out of the covenant.

Ellicott thinks the Chronicles form of the name probably correct as the more significant, and the variation here either a false reading or a change made to distinguish the king from Jeroboam’s son; he agrees that Abishalom is Absalom but adds that the queen mother is elsewhere called Michaiah and daughter of Uriel of Gibeah, which with the chronology shows she must have been Absalom’s granddaughter, and that of eighteen wives and threescore concubines she was the favourite; he infers from the qualified phrase about the heart that the king worshipped Jehovah only as the supreme God of his pantheon, and calls it a curious irony that he should be recorded inveighing against the degradation of that worship in Israel while conniving at rival gods in Judah; he takes the lamp for the victory that saved the house; he doubts the exception in David’s praise belongs to the text at all, since it appears here only and the Vatican and other Greek manuscripts omit it; and on the repeated war notice he concedes that the repetition seems inexplicable and the text probably in error. Keil and Delitzsch reckon the reign at two years and a few months rather than three full ones, meet the difficulty that the identical notice recurs of the next king’s mother by refusing the inference that a man had his own mother to wife, and harmonise the war notice by grammar, taking all the days of his life to mean so long as Abijam lived and reigned.

Gill makes the reign one whole year and part of two others, follows the Targum in reading the lamp as a kingdom continued in the king’s posterity, and harmonises the repeated war notice by referent, understanding the days of Abijam rather than Rehoboam, though some, he reports, take the son to be called by his father’s name.

Clarke says flatly that the king was an idolater who did not support the true worship, which he takes to be the general force of the phrase about an imperfect heart; cites Calmet for the usage by which Scripture calls granddaughter and daughter alike; makes the exception in David’s praise the one flagrant crime of his life, and not one offence but a whole system of them; and on the repeated war notice resorts to emendation, holding the true reading to be Abijam and citing fourteen of Kennicott’s and De Rossi’s manuscripts, the Syriac, the Arabic, the Targum and the first printed Vulgate.

debates.question: Why does the king’s name differ from the form used in Chronicles?

positions.view: A deliberate disgrace: the name of God is taken away where his faults are told
Either a false reading, or a change made to distinguish him from Jeroboam’s son

debates.question: How is the notice of war with Jeroboam, repeated from the previous chapter, to be explained?

positions.view: By grammar: all the days of his life means so long as Abijam lived and reigned
By referent: the days meant are Abijam’s, not Rehoboam’s
By emendation: the true reading is Abijam, on the authority of many manuscripts and versions
It cannot be explained; the text is probably in error

debates.question: Is the exception made in David’s praise original to the text?

positions.view: It is, and marks the one flagrant crime of his life
Probably not: it stands here alone, the Greek omits it, and it may be a marginal note or a compiler’s comment

outliers.claim: Alone in finding a curious irony in the king posing as champion of the Temple against the northern worship while conniving at rival gods at home.

9.pericope_label: Asa’s reforms: the consecrated persons, the queen mother’s idol, and the high places left standing

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch deny that the repeated notice of the mother can mean a man had his own mother to wife, note that Thenius finds that sense and builds emendations upon it, and hold instead, with Ephraem Syrus and the Rabbins, that she kept the standing of queen-mother through the next reign until deposed for idolatry, probably because the new king’s own mother had died young; on her idol they reject the obscene reading outright, since the word means formido, an idol as an object of fear, and not a shameful image as Movers explains it after the Rabbins. Ellicott agrees on the queen-mother’s standing; on the idol he holds the word, found only here and in its parallel, to mean a horrible abomination of some monstrous kind, reads for an asherah where the English has in a grove, and takes what replaced the ordinary wooden emblem to be of the sort often attached to nature-worship; and on the high places he finds in Chronicles an attempt at the reform that failed, the craving for local and visible sanctuaries proving too much for even earnest reformers.

Henry treats the forty-one years as the blessing of a good king and observes that the good reigns in Judah were generally the long ones, which makes the state of the church less bad than it first appears; he marks what it cost to go further, that idolatry found in the court was rooted out thence, for reformation must begin at home and bad practices are never suppressed in the country while supported at court, and presses the difficulty that the offender was the king’s own grandmother, whom he loved well but loved God better, forgetting the relation like the Levite when it came into competition with his duty; on the idol he stays with the act, which was publicly exposed, defaced and burnt by the brook Kidron; and on the high places he allows that every rival image was removed but the altars left, being loth to disoblige the people, then argues that they were contrary to the law, lessened men’s esteem of the temple and stood open as a gap for idolatry — concluding that a heart may be perfect with God, meaning sincere rather than sinless, while falling short of good it might have done.

Clarke renders the term for the consecrated persons literally, cites Calmet on the breadth of the word daughter, and collates six renderings of the word for the queen mother’s idol — Vulgate, Greek, Syriac, Chaldee, Arabic and Jarchi — concluding that the thing was an obscene emblem and that she held an assembly in the grove where it stood; on the high places he says the king could not make a thorough reformation, that being left to his son, and reports Jarchi’s view that those left standing were raised by individuals for the worship of Jehovah.

Gill has the consecrated persons either driven out or put to death according to the law, as many as came to the king’s knowledge, since some remained; and takes the high places for sites used in God’s worship before the temple was built, which the king may have thought still lawful, or which the people’s attachment made dangerous to touch.

debates.question: What was the queen mother’s idol?

positions.view: An obscene emblem, on the drift of the ancient versions
A horrible abomination of some monstrous kind, set up for an asherah, of the sort attached to nature-worship
Not a shameful image at all: the word means an object of fear, and the reading of Movers after the Rabbins is to be rejected

debates.question: Why were the high places left standing?

positions.view: They had served in God’s worship before the temple, so may have seemed lawful, or were too dear to the people to touch
The king was simply unable to carry a thorough reformation, which was left to his son
The reform was attempted and failed, the craving for local sanctuaries defeating even earnest reformers
He thought no great harm in them and was loth to disoblige the people, though they were against the law

outliers.claim: Alone in rejecting the obscene reading of the queen mother’s idol, holding the word to mean an object of fear rather than a shameful image.
Alone in drawing from the deposition the rule that reformation must begin at home, since bad practices are never suppressed in the country while they are supported at court.

16.pericope_label: Baasha fortifies Ramah; Asa buys Syrian help with the temple treasure and is rebuked

schools.summary: Gill counts the thirty-six years from the division of the kingdom rather than the accession — seventeen under Rehoboam, three under Abijam — which brings the invasion to Asa’s sixteenth year, following the Jewish chronology; he also reports Abarbinel’s reason for the king of Israel being named here out of order, that the historian relates Asa’s failings after his good deeds and before the rest of his history.

Keil and Delitzsch reach the sixteenth year from the Chronicles sequence of ten years’ rest, the Cushite invasion in the eleventh and the thanksgiving in the fifteenth; they mark the inconsistency that the king who sought the Lord’s help against the Cushites sought Syrian help against Israel; and they have the Syrian captains take the northern cities and so compel Baasha to abandon the building and withdraw to his capital, locating the two places afterwards fortified from the spoil. Ellicott takes the standing phrase about war to mean only that the old hostile relations continued, open war not breaking out until after the victory over Zerah; he puts Ramah five miles north of the capital, identifies it with a village standing there still, and compares the move to the fortifying of Decelea near Athens in the Peloponnesian war, a standing menace beside a hostile capital; he weighs the alliance as policy and as faith together, calling it the first calling in of a heathen power against his brethren the children of Israel, a desperate expedient and an unfaithfulness to a brotherhood separation had not dissolved; and on the disease of the king’s old age he adds from Chronicles that he sought the physicians and not the Lord, and went so far as to imprison the seer who rebuked him.

Clarke leaves the chronology open, holding that either the chronologers’ reckoning from the separation of the kingdoms must be adopted or there is a mistake in some of the numbers, most likely in the parallel places, which he says we have no means of correcting; he takes Ramah for a hill commanding the defile through which the chief road to Jerusalem ran, fortified to stop all intercourse lest the northern subjects cleave to David’s house; he is harsher than the others about the motive for the alliance, since no danger threatened which the king could not have turned aside himself, so that he probably meant to destroy the northern kingdom outright and robbed the house of the Lord to do it; and he draws a maxim from the levy no man was exempted from, that where boundaries must be fortified against an enemy all exemptions cease.

Henry lists three faults in the alliance: that the king tempted Benhadad to break a league and violate the public faith; that he could not trust the God who had already delivered him; and that he took gold from a treasury not to be touched save on extraordinary occasions. He grants that the design prospered and yet displeased God, the king being told by the prophet that he had done foolishly and should thenceforth have wars; and he says of the disease only that the gout made him peevish with those about him.

debates.question: How is the invasion dated, given that the thirty-sixth year named in Chronicles falls after Baasha’s death?

positions.view: The years count from the division of the kingdom, which brings it to Asa’s sixteenth year
The sixteenth year, as the sequence of events in Chronicles requires
The standing phrase means only continued hostility; open war began after the victory over Zerah
Either the chronologers’ reckoning must be adopted, or some of the numbers are mistaken and cannot now be corrected

debates.question: What was the worst of the Syrian alliance?

positions.view: Three things: tempting a king to break faith, distrusting God, and spending treasure reserved for extraordinary need
The motive: no danger compelled it, so the king meant conquest and robbed the house of the Lord for it
Calling in a heathen power against his own brethren, an unfaithfulness to a brotherhood separation had not dissolved

outliers.claim: Alone in comparing the fortifying of Ramah beside the hostile capital to the fortifying of Decelea near Athens in the Peloponnesian war.
Alone in drawing from the general levy a maxim of civil policy, that where boundaries must be fortified against an enemy all exemptions cease.

25.pericope_label: Nadab killed at Gibbethon, the house of Jeroboam extirpated, and Baasha’s reign

schools.summary: Henry counts six or seven hands holding the northern government during the single reign of Asa — Jeroboam at the beginning and Ahab at the end, with Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Tibni and Omri undermining one another between — and takes it for the fulfilment of the threat that they should be as a reed shaken in the water, got by deserting the house both of God and of David; he notes a chance thrown away in the son who was killed, since a brother’s death might have made him religious; he will not decide between personal pique, revenge for an affront, a pretence of freeing the country from a bad prince, and plain ambition as the conspirator’s motive; and he adds the detail that condemns the murdered king more than the murder does, that his army not only did not avenge his death but chose his murderer to succeed him.

Ellicott makes Baasha the first of the many military chiefs who seized the throne of Israel by violence or assassination, and sets the constant succession of ephemeral dynasties against the unchanged royalty of David’s house resting on the promise of God; he takes the recurring formula about doing evil to mean perseverance in the system Jeroboam introduced; on Gibbethon he reads a Philistine revolt against the enfeebled power of Israel, notes that the place commanded a pass from the plain of Sharon inland, and observes that the siege must have been fruitless of lasting result since twenty-six years later the town is still in enemy hands; and he denies the conspirator any formal commission of vengeance, inferring from the later judgment pronounced on him that the killing was itself a sin, and drawing the conclusion that sin which works out God’s purpose is not the less truly sin. Keil and Delitzsch note that the prophet’s words against this house coincide exactly, with the necessary changes, with those against Jeroboam’s, remark on the strange perversity of kings who had seen the families before them overthrown for the calf-worship and then worshipped the same calves, and observe that the notice of war with Judah is simply a repetition of what the chapter has already said.

Gill guesses the conspirator an officer of the army whose chief view was the kingdom, turns the providence against him, since he destroyed the family not from any dislike of Jeroboam’s sins, in which he walked himself, but because the Lord had threatened it, observes that the whole kingdom submitted to a usurper and murderer, and accounts for the standing hostility with Judah by the impossibility of any good understanding between them.

Clarke calls Gibbethon a city of Dan generally in Philistine hands, puts the providence flatly in saying that God made use of one wicked man to destroy another, and draws the rule that the entail of iniquity cannot be cut off but by a thorough conversion of the soul to God, of which these kings seem to have had no adequate notion, so that the wicked followed the steps of the wicked and grew worse, sin gathering strength by exercise and age.

debates.question: What moved Baasha to conspire against Nadab?

positions.view: It cannot be decided among personal pique, revenge, a pretence of public good, and ambition
Ambition: he was an army officer whose chief view was the kingdom

debates.question: How is the extirpation of Jeroboam’s house to be judged?

positions.view: God made use of one wicked man to destroy another
The executioner acted from no dislike of the sins he punished, walking in them himself; the Lord had threatened it and suffered it
Sin which works out God’s purpose is not the less truly sin, and judgment fell on him in part for the killing

outliers.claim: Alone in proving the siege of Gibbethon fruitless from a notice twenty-six years later that the town is still in enemy hands.
Alone in remarking on the perversity of kings who had themselves overthrown dynasties judged for the calf-worship and then kept up that worship.
